problem: End-to-end visual navigation policies (ViNT, NoMaD, PlaceNav, FAINT) output robot-specific actions, are trained only on same-trajectory start/goal pairs, and rely on a single retrieved subgoal image. They therefore break under camera mismatch, off-trajectory starts and backward traversal.
motivation: Reference RGB trajectories (e.g. phone videos) are an easy way to specify routes, but the deployed robot often has a different camera, embodiment and viewpoint. Decoupling perception from action, by predicting where the trajectory appears in the current image, gives a robot-agnostic interface for classical planners. It also allows training on cross-trajectory pairs without action labels.
key_idea: Learn to localize all poses of a reference RGB trajectory in the robot's current image (2D point, visibility, normalized distance) by jointly processing the whole trajectory, and let a simple local controller track those points.
insight: Predicting image-space trajectory localization instead of actions allows cross-trajectory and cross-camera training, which yields robustness to camera mismatch and to opposing views (backward traversal), even though the training data contains no backward demonstrations. The ablation of full-trajectory vs frame-wise processing (Single) shows drops of ~25-33 SR points on backward traversal and up to ~26 on off-trajectory forward. Frame-wise matching degrades with initialization distance toward the FAINT curve, so joint trajectory processing is what enables far-off starts.
method: Guidance representation: for each reference frame predict a 2D point in the query image (normalized [-1,1]), a visibility logit, and a normalized distance (farthest visible point = 1).

Trajectory encoder E_T: frozen DINOv3 ViT-B features projected to D=256, a summary token per frame, 12 alternating global/frame-wise attention blocks with spatial+temporal RoPE. Run once offline per trajectory.

Query encoder + fusion: 6 self-attention layers for the query image; a 6-block decoder where trajectory tokens cross-attend to query tokens, alternating with frame-wise self-attention that aggregates correspondences into summary tokens.

Prediction head: recurrent transformer with K=4 iterations, AdaLN conditioning on the previous estimate, self-attention across all N frames' summary tokens, residual updates; tanh outputs for coordinates and distance.

Cross-trajectory training: reference and query sampled from different real trajectories, plus Habitat sim data with randomized FOV/aspect/height and rotation perturbations. GT from camera-center projection with depth-based occlusion check; L1 pos + BCE vis + L1 dist losses with RAFT-style weighting over iterations.

Controllers: (1) yaw P-controller with constant forward velocity steering to the visible point nearest the robot (plus lookahead toward goal index); optional reactive obstacle avoidance. (2) Perception-aware MPPI for a drone, grounding points in 3D with UniDepthV2 depth, with goal, visibility and collision costs.

setting.backbone: Frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/14 + custom ~50M-parameter transformer (trained from scratch); classical yaw/MPPI controllers
setting.training_data: ~25,000 reference trajectories (up to 40 frames) and 850k query images across 500 environments: sim (HM3D, HSSD, AI2-THOR via Habitat) plus real (CODa, LILocBench, BotanicGarden, TartanGround); ~4 days on one RTX 5090
setting.observation: monocular RGB (query image + reference RGB trajectory, unposed, no calibration), resized to 224x224
setting.action_space: Model outputs image-space points; controller gives yaw rate with constant forward velocity (Spot/sim), or MPPI velocity/yaw commands (Crazyflie)
setting.simulator: Habitat (Gibson, HM3D) for evaluation; real world
setting.privileged: none at test time (depth used only in training labels; UniDepthV2 predicted depth for MPPI drone)

results: With only a yaw controller, LoTIS reaches 94.7% (Gibson) and 98.5% (HM3D) SR on forward on-trajectory navigation, beating the best baseline (ViNT, 70.4/65.7) by ~24-33 points. With obstacle avoidance it reaches 94-100% in most settings. On backward traversal the baselines fail (<~12% SR) while LoTIS gets 65-88% (87-97% with avoidance). In real-world trials it succeeds 100% forward and 94.4% backward vs FAINT's 27.8% and 5.6%.
limitations: Requires visual overlap between current view and some part of the reference trajectory; fails around sharp corners or under extreme viewpoint changes, and degrades with large camera height mismatch.

Real-world evaluation is limited to four environments (36 runs per method); trajectories up to ~100 m subsampled to 40 frames, and longer trajectories need chunking that is not systematically evaluated.
Navigation to unseen goals or semantic goals is out of scope; there is no temporal memory to recover when the trajectory leaves the view.
